name: Radivoj Korać
milestone_by_age_26: Became top scorer of the Yugoslav First Federal League in 1957 at age 18, the first of a record seven consecutive top-scorer titles.
early_history_summary: Korać started playing basketball at age 12 during a family vacation and joined OKK Beograd at 16. He debuted in the Yugoslav First Federal League in 1957 and immediately became its top scorer, a feat he repeated for seven consecutive seasons.
family_context_summary: Born to Bogdan, a post office clerk, and Zagorka in Sombor; father was imprisoned on Goli Otok for two years, and the family endured wartime displacement before settling in Belgrade.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early club access, physical edge, teammate synergy, adversity
evidence_summary: Korać grew up in modest circumstances in post-war Belgrade, near the OKK Beograd courts. He started basketball at 12, joined the club at 16, and became the Yugoslav League's top scorer at 18 — the first of seven consecutive titles. His father's imprisonment and wartime family displacement created hardship but also urgency. His exceptional left-handed scoring and physical stature (196cm) set him apart from the start.
starting_point: Born to a modest family in Sombor, Yugoslavia; father was a post office clerk who was later imprisoned on Goli Otok, and the family endured wartime displacement before settling in Belgrade.
current_position: Died in a car crash on June 2, 1969 at age 30 in Sarajevo; final role was player for Petrarca Padova and the Yugoslavia national team.

trajectory.event: Joined OKK Beograd, beginning his senior club career.
Became top scorer of the Yugoslav First Federal League, the first of seven consecutive top-scorer titles.
Named Best Athlete of Yugoslavia and top scorer at the Rome Olympics.
Won EuroBasket MVP and EuroBasket Top Scorer honors.
Scored 99 points in a single EuroLeague game, setting an all-time record that still stands.
Won Olympic silver medal at the Mexico City Games with Yugoslavia.
Died in a car accident near Sarajevo on June 2, 1969.

name: George Maciunas
milestone_by_age_26: Was still a student at Cooper Union and Carnegie Tech through his mid-twenties; founded Fluxus in 1962 at age 30-31, with no material artistic milestone by age 26.
early_history_summary: Maciunas studied art, graphic design, architecture, and musicology at Cooper Union, Carnegie Tech, and NYU from 1949 to 1960. His first significant artistic organizing work came with the AG Gallery in 1960 and the Fluxus movement beginning in 1962.
family_context_summary: Born to Alexander Maciunas, a Lithuanian architect and engineer trained in Berlin, and Leokadija, a Russian-born dancer with the Lithuanian National Opera; middle-class family that emigrated to the US in 1948.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an architect and engineer; mother was a dancer with the Lithuanian National Opera, providing an arts-adjacent family environment.

name: Gaël Monfils
milestone_by_age_26: Reached world No. 1 junior ranking in February 2004 and won three of four junior Grand Slam singles titles (Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon) at age 17, becoming ITF youth world champion.
early_history_summary: Monfils started playing tennis as a child in Paris, coached initially by his father. He compiled an 83-22 junior record and dominated the 2004 junior season, winning three junior Grand Slams and reaching the No. 1 junior world ranking before turning professional.
family_context_summary: Born to Rufin Monfils, a former pro footballer from Guadeloupe who worked at France Telecom, and Sylvette Cartesse, a nurse from Martinique; parents divorced during his youth, and his mother worked night shifts to support his tennis.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Rufin was a former professional football player who introduced Monfils to tennis and served as his early coach.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father-coach, physical edge, French tennis system, junior circuit
evidence_summary: Monfils grew up in a working-class Parisian family with Caribbean roots; his father, a former pro footballer, introduced him to tennis and coached him early. He was also a gifted sprinter, winning French youth 100m titles. By 17, he dominated junior tennis, winning three junior Grand Slams and reaching No. 1 junior world ranking. His mother worked night shifts as a nurse to support his development.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family in Paris; father was a former pro footballer from Guadeloupe working at France Telecom, mother was a nurse from Martinique who worked night shifts to support his tennis.
current_position: Active ATP Tour player at age 38-39; married to WTA player Elina Svitolina; resides in Switzerland; career prize money approximately $20+ million.

trajectory.event: Became world No. 1 junior, winning three junior Grand Slam titles and the ITF youth world champion title.
Won first ATP title at the Sopot Open and broke into the ATP top 30.
Reached the French Open semifinals, losing to Roger Federer.
Reached the US Open semifinals and achieved a career-high ranking of world No. 6.
Married WTA player Elina Svitolina; became a father.
Continued competing on the ATP Tour, becoming one of the oldest active players.

name: Michael Jordan
milestone_by_age_26: Hit the game-winning shot in the 1982 NCAA Championship game as a freshman at UNC at age 19, later winning national college player of the year (1984), Olympic gold (1984), and NBA Rookie of the Year (1985) — all before age 23.
early_history_summary: Jordan grew up in Wilmington, NC, cut from his high school varsity team as a sophomore before growing four inches and becoming a McDonald's All-American. At UNC, he hit the iconic game-winning shot in the 1982 NCAA Championship as a freshman, launching his career.
family_context_summary: Born to James Jordan, an equipment supervisor at a General Electric plant and Air Force veteran, and Deloris Jordan, a bank employee; raised in a stable middle-class household in Wilmington, NC with four siblings.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father James built a backyard basketball court and introduced Jordan to sports, though no family member had professional basketball background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UNC/Dean Smith, backyard court, sibling rivalry, physical edge, varsity cut motivation
evidence_summary: Jordan grew up in a stable middle-class family in Wilmington, NC; his father built a backyard basketball court where Jordan developed his game competing fiercely against his older brother Larry. After being cut from the varsity team as a sophomore, he grew four inches and became a McDonald's All-American. At UNC, he hit the game-winning shot in the 1982 NCAA Championship as a freshman under coach Dean Smith, a pivotal moment he described as the major turning point in his career.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class family in Brooklyn, NY; father was an equipment supervisor at General Electric and Air Force veteran, mother was a bank employee; family moved to Wilmington, NC when Jordan was five.
current_position: Minority owner of the Charlotte Hornets; net worth approximately $4.3 billion as of 2026; co-owner of 23XI Racing in NASCAR; widely considered the greatest basketball player of all time.

trajectory.event: Named McDonald's All-American after averaging 26.8 ppg as a high school senior at Laney High School.
Hit the game-winning shot in the NCAA Championship game as a freshman at UNC, winning the national title.
Won national college player of the year, Olympic gold in Los Angeles, and was drafted 3rd overall by the Chicago Bulls.
Named NBA Rookie of the Year after averaging 28.2 ppg and becoming an All-Star starter.
Won NBA MVP and Defensive Player of the Year, averaging 35.0 ppg.
Won his first NBA championship with the Chicago Bulls, followed by two more in 1992 and 1993.
Returned from baseball retirement to lead the Bulls to a then-record 72-win season and fourth NBA title.
Became the first billionaire player in NBA history as Hornets owner.

name: Bruno Habārovs
milestone_by_age_26: Won the individual épée gold medal at the 1959 World Fencing Championships at age 20, also winning junior world champion that same year.
early_history_summary: Habārovs trained at Dynamo Riga under coach Sergejs Habarovs and won the Soviet junior championship in 1958 before breaking through internationally with individual gold at the 1959 World Championships.
family_context_summary: Born in Riga, Latvia; his coach was listed as Sergejs Habarovs, suggesting a possible family connection to fencing, though family background is not well documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Coach Sergejs Habarovs shares the surname, suggesting possible family involvement in fencing training, though this is not confirmed in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, Dynamo Riga, family coach, early specialization
evidence_summary: Habārovs trained at Dynamo Riga under coach Sergejs Habarovs, who shares his surname, suggesting possible family involvement in his fencing development. He won the Soviet junior championship in 1958 and then became individual épée world champion at age 20 in 1959, also winning junior world champion that year. The Soviet sports system provided structured training and competition pathways.
starting_point: Born in Riga, Latvia; trained under coach Sergejs Habarovs (possibly a family member) at Dynamo Riga.
current_position: Died on August 29, 1994 at age 55 in Riga; final role was fencing coach and sports instructor after graduating from LVFKI in 1966.

trajectory.event: Won the Soviet junior fencing championship in épée.
Won individual épée gold at the World Championships and was named junior world champion.
Won two bronze medals (individual and team épée) at the Rome Olympics.
Won team épée gold at the World Championships in Turin.
Won team épée bronze at the World Championships and two Universiade silver medals.
Died in Riga on August 29, 1994.

name: Tijana Bošković
milestone_by_age_26: Debuted for Serbia's senior national team at the 2014 FIVB World Championship at age 17, becoming the team's leading scorer, after winning U19 European Championship gold the same year.
early_history_summary: Bošković started with karate before focusing on volleyball, following her older sister Dajana. At 14, she moved to Belgrade with her sister to train, joining Vizura/Partizan. She quickly rose through junior national teams and debuted for the senior national team at 17.
family_context_summary: Born to Serb parents in Trebinje, Bosnia and Herzegovina; older sister Dajana plays for the Bosnia national volleyball team, and younger brother Vuk is a basketball player; moved to Belgrade at 14 with her sister to pursue volleyball.
parent_family_domain_summary: Older sister Dajana was a volleyball player who paved the path; the family supported both sisters moving to Belgrade at young ages for volleyball training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: sister pathfinder, Serbian volleyball system, physical edge, early national team
evidence_summary: Bošković grew up in Trebinje, Bosnia, where she initially tried karate before following her older sister Dajana into volleyball. At 14, she moved to Belgrade with her sister to train at Vizura/Partizan. Her exceptional physical profile (193cm, left-handed opposite) was immediately apparent, and she rose through junior national teams rapidly. At 17, she debuted for Serbia's senior national team at the 2014 World Championship as the team's leading scorer, also winning U19 European Championship gold that year.
starting_point: Born to Serb parents in Trebinje, Bosnia and Herzegovina; older sister Dajana was a volleyball player who provided a path into the sport; moved to Belgrade at 14 with her sister to pursue volleyball seriously.
current_position: Plays for VakıfBank in Turkey; widely considered one of the world's best volleyball players; two-time world champion (2018, 2022), two-time European champion, and two-time Olympic medalist (silver 2016, bronze 2020).

trajectory.event: Won silver at the European Youth Olympic Festival, earning MVP and Best Spiker honors.
Debuted for Serbia's senior national team at the World Championship and won U19 European Championship gold.
Won Olympic silver at the Rio de Janeiro Games and the FIVB Club World Championship with Eczacibasi, earning MVP.
Led Serbia to World Championship gold, earning tournament MVP honors.
Won European Championship gold with Serbia and was named CEV Female Volleyball Player of the Year for the third consecutive time.
Won her second World Championship gold with Serbia.
Continued playing for VakıfBank as one of the highest-profile volleyball players in the world.

name: Ruslan Ponomariov
milestone_by_age_26: Became FIDE World Chess Champion in 2002 at age 18, the youngest holder of the title in history, after becoming the youngest grandmaster ever at 14 in 1998.
early_history_summary: Ponomariov was taught chess by his father at age 5, moved to Kramatorsk at 9 to attend the A.V. Momot Chess School, and progressed rapidly: European U18 champion at 12, World U18 champion at 13, youngest grandmaster ever at 14, and FIDE World Champion at 18.
family_context_summary: Born in Horlivka, Ukraine; taught chess by his father at age 5; moved to Kramatorsk at 9 to attend a specialized chess school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father taught him chess at age 5, initiating his path in the game.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father-taught, specialized chess school, prodigy, early GM, Ukrainian chess culture
evidence_summary: Ponomariov was taught chess by his father at age 5 and moved to Kramatorsk at 9 to attend the elite A.V. Momot Chess School, which has produced multiple top grandmasters. He progressed at an extraordinary rate: European U18 champion at 12, World U18 champion at 13, and the youngest grandmaster in history at 14 in 1998. At 18, he won the FIDE World Chess Championship, becoming the youngest holder of the title.
starting_point: Born in Horlivka, Ukraine; father taught him chess at age 5; family moved to Kramatorsk at age 9 for specialized chess training.
current_position: Active chess grandmaster; FIDE rating 2632 (July 2026); peak rating 2764 (July 2011); former FIDE world champion residing in Ukraine.

trajectory.event: Won the World U18 Chess Championship at age 13.
Became the youngest grandmaster in history at age 14, a record at the time.
Won the FIDE World Chess Championship, defeating Vasyl Ivanchuk in the final to become the youngest ever FIDE world champion.
Won gold medal with Ukraine at the Chess Olympiad in Calvia.
Reached the final of the FIDE World Cup.
Achieved peak rating of 2764 and won the Ukrainian Chess Championship.
Continued competing as an active grandmaster, ranked approximately 95th in the world.

name: Radomir Antić
milestone_by_age_26: Was a regular defender for Partizan Belgrade by age 22 but won his first league title at 27-28 (1976); his major achievements as a player and manager all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Antić started his playing career at Sloboda Titovo Užice (1967-1970) before moving to Partizan (1970-1977), where he was a regular defender. He earned one cap for Yugoslavia in 1973 but won his first league title only in 1976 at age 27-28.
family_context_summary: Born in Žitište, PR Serbia, FPR Yugoslavia; family background not documented in reviewed sources.

name: František Ševčík
milestone_by_age_26: Won a silver medal at the 1965 World Ice Hockey Championships with Czechoslovakia at age 23, his first of four World Championship medals, and was a five-time league champion with Rudá hvězda/ZKL Brno.
early_history_summary: Ševčík started playing hockey in his hometown of Vilémovice and debuted in the top Czechoslovak league with Rudá hvězda Brno in 1961 at age 19. He won five league titles with Brno and was first called up to the national team for the 1965 World Championships, where he won silver.
family_context_summary: Born in Vilémovice, a small village in the Blansko district of Moravia; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Rudá hvězda Brno, Czechoslovak hockey system, team collective
evidence_summary: Ševčík grew up in the small Moravian village of Vilémovice and started playing hockey there before joining Rudá hvězda Brno, one of Czechoslovakia's dominant clubs, in 1961 at age 19. He won five league titles with Brno and was first called up to the national team for the 1965 World Championships, where he contributed four goals and three assists to win silver. The Czechoslovak hockey system provided a structured pathway from club to national team.
starting_point: Born in the small village of Vilémovice in Moravia; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on July 22, 2017 at age 75 in Brno; had worked as a financial and operational director for Boby Brno football club after retiring from hockey.

trajectory.event: Debuted in the top Czechoslovak hockey league with Rudá hvězda Brno.
Won silver medal at the World Championships, his first national team call-up, scoring four goals and three assists.
Won his second World Championship silver medal with Czechoslovakia.
Won Olympic silver medal at the Grenoble Winter Games and was named to the Olympic All-Star team.
Won World Championship bronze medal with Czechoslovakia.
Left Brno after 12 seasons to join Baník Karviná.
Died on July 22, 2017 in Brno.

name: Robert H. MacArthur
milestone_by_age_26: Published one paper in Ecology in 1955 at age 25, but his landmark contributions — the PhD thesis on warbler niche partitioning (1957), 'On Bird Species Diversity' (1961), and 'The Theory of Island Biogeography' (1967) — all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: MacArthur earned a BA from Marlboro College, an AM in mathematics from Brown (1953), and was a PhD student at Yale under G. Evelyn Hutchinson. His first publication appeared in 1955, but his landmark doctoral work on warbler niche partitioning was completed in 1957 at age 27.
family_context_summary: Born to John Wood MacArthur, a professor of genetics at the University of Toronto and Marlboro College, and Olive Turner; youngest son in an academic family with an older brother who was a physicist.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a professor of genetics, providing direct academic domain proximity and intellectual environment from childhood.

name: Ulay
milestone_by_age_26: Was completing photography studies and starting work as a Polaroid consultant in Amsterdam by age 25-26; his first significant artistic works (Renais Sense series, 1974) and collaboration with Marina Abramović (1975 onwards) came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Ulay studied photography from 1962 to 1968 and moved to Amsterdam in 1968 at age 24-25, where he worked as a consultant for Polaroid. His first notable artistic works emerged in the early 1970s, with the Renais Sense series in 1974 and the beginning of his collaboration with Marina Abramović in 1975.
family_context_summary: Born Frank Uwe Laysiepen in Solingen, Germany; family background not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Harry Kane
milestone_by_age_26: Named PFA Young Player of the Year for the 2014-15 Premier League season at age 21-22, having scored 21 league goals in his breakout season for Tottenham Hotspur.
early_history_summary: Kane played for Ridgeway Rovers from age 6, was briefly in Arsenal's academy (released at 9), and joined Tottenham's academy at 11. After loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich, and Leicester, he broke into Tottenham's first team under Pochettino in 2014-15, scoring 21 league goals and winning PFA Young Player of the Year.
family_context_summary: Born to Patrick Kane, born in Galway, Ireland, and Kim (née Hogg) in Leytonstone, London; raised in Walthamstow then Chingford; working/middle-class family with grandfather Eric on mother's side being 'quite a good footballer.'
parent_family_domain_summary: Grandfather Eric (maternal) was described by Kane as 'quite a good footballer' who played at a decent level; father played football with Kane and his brother in the park.
primary_early_advantage_tags: backyard football, sibling rivalry, academy rejection motivation, North London football culture, Tottenham proximity
evidence_summary: Kane grew up in a working/middle-class family in Chingford, North London, 15 minutes from White Hart Lane. He played football from age 6, initially at Ridgeway Rovers (which also produced David Beckham), and was briefly in Arsenal's academy before being released at 9 for being 'a bit chubby.' After joining Tottenham's academy at 11, he developed through loan spells across the English football pyramid before breaking out in 2014-15 with 21 Premier League goals and the PFA Young Player of the Year award at 21. His grandfather was a decent footballer, and his older brother was a constant competitive partner.
starting_point: Born to a working/middle-class family in Leytonstone, London; father was born in Galway, Ireland; family lived in Walthamstow then Chingford, 15 minutes from Tottenham's White Hart Lane.
current_position: Plays for Bayern Munich in the Bundesliga; England's all-time top goalscorer (85 goals); net worth estimated at approximately $50-60 million; won first major trophy (Bundesliga) in 2024-25 season.

trajectory.event: Made professional debut on loan at Leyton Orient, scoring five goals in 18 appearances.
Named PFA Young Player of the Year after scoring 21 Premier League goals in his breakout Tottenham season.
Won the Premier League Golden Boot with 25 goals and helped Tottenham to a third-place finish.
Won the World Cup Golden Boot as top scorer at the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia.
Reached the Champions League final with Tottenham, finishing as runner-up to Liverpool.
Joined Bayern Munich for a record €110 million fee, becoming the most expensive signing in Bundesliga history.
Won the European Golden Shoe in his debut Bundesliga season with 36 league goals.
Won his first major trophy, the Bundesliga title, and was named Bundesliga Player of the Season.
